Data loading::Integrating with Query.summary: Use TanStack Router loaders to await TanStack Query data while Query owns the cache. This coordinates navigation without maintaining a duplicate router cache.
Data loading::Integrating with Query.explanation: TanStack Router can coordinate TanStack Query by receiving a QueryClient through router context and awaiting its query-loading API in a route loader. The component then reads the same query options, so the query library owns caching and freshness instead of the router maintaining a second copy.
Data loading::Integrating with Query.returns: The route loader returns the promise from the QueryClient loading operation; the integration handles SSR dehydration, hydration, and streaming.

example.title: Await query data in a route loader
example.explanation: The route loader ensures the query is available before rendering, while the component reads the same cache entry through TanStack Query.

useCases.title: Navigation-gated data loading
useCases.scenario: A route needs critical server data before its component renders.

useCases.title: Shared query cache
useCases.scenario: Several routes share server state and need freshness, deduplication, or background updates.

useCases.title: SSR hydration and streaming
useCases.scenario: An SSR application must transfer loaded query data to the browser.

interview.question: How should TanStack Router and TanStack Query be combined without duplicating a cache?
interview.answer: Use the route loader to await the QueryClient's query-loading method, then read that query in the component with the same query key and function. This lets Query own the cache while the router coordinates navigation readiness.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid duplicate providers? Pass wrapQueryClient: false to the integration and retain the application's existing QueryClientProvider.

interview.question: What does the official SSR Query integration provide?
interview.answer: Install the integration package, create a QueryClient, put it in router context, and call setupRouterSsrQueryIntegration with the router and client. The integration handles SSR dehydration and hydration, and can also stream queries during initial rendering.
interview.followUp: What must change for SSR request isolation? Construct the QueryClient inside the per-request router factory rather than at module scope.

interview.question: How do useSuspenseQuery and useQuery differ in SSR?
interview.answer: useSuspenseQuery can run during SSR when its data is required and stream the result as it resolves. Plain useQuery does not execute on the server and instead fetches after hydration on the client.
interview.followUp: How can serialization behavior be customized? Supply dehydrateOptions and hydrateOptions to the integration.

keyPoints: Treat the router as the navigation coordinator and let TanStack Query remain responsible for server-state caching.
Use Query's prefetching or cache-reading API in place of a router-specific fetch implementation.
Read the result through the query library's hook or read-or-fetch API rather than creating a second router cache.
The dedicated integration connects the two libraries for server rendering, hydration, and streaming.
The integration can handle redirects thrown by query or mutation operations when redirect handling is enabled.
gotchas: Create a new QueryClient for every server request; sharing one across requests can leak cached data between users.
If the application already supplies its own provider, disable the integration wrapper rather than mounting two providers.
Do not assume useQuery performs server-side loading during SSR; useSuspenseQuery is the documented server-rendered alternative.

Data loading::loaderDeps.summary: loaderDeps declares which validated search parameters identify a route's loaded data. When the returned dependencies change, TanStack Router reloads the route and exposes them to the loader as deps.
Data loading::loaderDeps.explanation: Define loaderDeps as a pure function over validated search parameters, return the values that identify the loader's data, and read that returned object through the loader's deps argument. TanStack Router compares the returned dependencies deeply; a change triggers reloading even when staleTimes would otherwise keep the route fresh.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Object containing the route's validated search values.

Data loading::loaderDeps.returns: A serializable dependency value, typically an object, that uniquely identifies the route match and is supplied to the loader as deps.

example.title: Reload a paginated loader
example.explanation: The validated pagination values become loader dependencies, so the route reloads and caches separately when either value changes.

useCases.title: Paginated data
useCases.scenario: A list endpoint changes its response for different page offsets or page sizes.

useCases.title: Filtered and sorted results
useCases.scenario: The same route loads different records based on validated filter or sort values.

useCases.title: Search-specific caching
useCases.scenario: A search-dependent resource must have separate route-cache identities for each query.

interview.question: What is loaderDeps and how does the loader use it?
interview.answer: loaderDeps is an optional callback receiving the route's validated search schema. It returns a serializable dependency object that identifies the route match and is exposed to the loader as deps.
interview.followUp: What happens when the returned object changes? The router compares dependencies with deep equality and reloads the route when they differ.

interview.question: How should search parameters be connected to a loader?
interview.answer: Use loaderDeps to select search parameters that affect the loaded data, such as pagination, sorting, or filters. The loader then reads those selected values from its deps argument.
interview.followUp: Why not read arbitrary search values directly in the loader? Declaring them makes them part of route-match identity and cache behavior, so changes reliably trigger loading.

interview.question: What constraints apply to a loaderDeps return value?
interview.answer: The callback should be deterministic, side-effect-free, and return a serializable value. Path parameters normally need not be returned because they already identify the route match.
interview.followUp: Can the dependency value be an arbitrary object? It may be any serializable value, provided it uniquely identifies the match and its serialization is also side-effect-free.

keyPoints: loaderDeps runs before route matching and adds search-derived identity to the route match.
Nested dependency values are compared deeply rather than only by object reference.
Search parameters that distinguish the loaded resource must be returned so the loader can receive them through deps.
Include every search value that changes the fetched result to keep cached entries distinct.
gotchas: Return a serializable identity for every search value that changes the loader's result; otherwise distinct data can share a route match or cache entry.
Do not duplicate path parameters in loaderDeps because the router already includes them in route-match identity.
Avoid timestamps, random values, mutations, and external effects: the same validated search input must produce the same dependencies.

Data loading::Pending and error componen.summary: Define pendingComponent and errorComponent on a route to keep loading and failure UI at the route's own data boundary. The router falls back through parent boundaries to its default error component when needed.
Data loading::Pending and error componen.explanation: A route can define pendingComponent for slow loader work and errorComponent for failures. During navigation, the router uses the route's boundary first; if it is absent, the corresponding parent or router-level default can handle the state.

parameters.name: routeOptions
parameters.description: Route option containing the loader and optional pendingComponent/errorComponent boundaries.

Data loading::Pending and error componen.returns: The configured route components render the route's loading or error state during data loading.

example.title: Route-owned pending and error UI
example.explanation: The route supplies its own loading and failure UI while its loader is pending or throws.

useCases.title: Show route-specific loading UI
useCases.scenario: A route loader takes longer than the pending threshold.

useCases.title: Render local failure UI
useCases.scenario: A route loader rejects or throws during navigation.

useCases.title: Keep boundaries close to route behavior
useCases.scenario: Different route branches need distinct loading and error presentation.

interview.question: How does a route declare pending and error UI?
interview.answer: Define pendingComponent and errorComponent in the route options. The pending component is used when loading exceeds the pending threshold; an error component handles loader errors.
interview.followUp: What happens if the route has no local error component? The router falls back to the parent route's errorComponent and then the router default.

interview.question: How are loader errors assigned to boundaries?
interview.answer: The router processes route loading in parallel and associates loader failures with the route error boundary chain. It renders the route's error component when configured, otherwise it searches ancestors and then the router default.
interview.followUp: Which settings control when pending UI appears? routeOptions.pendingMs or routerOptions.defaultPendingMs control the threshold.

interview.question: Why might a pending component not appear immediately?
interview.answer: Pending UI is not necessarily immediate: the default pending threshold is one second, and the pending view has a default minimum display time of 500 milliseconds. Both values are configurable.
interview.followUp: How can an application avoid showing a fallback for a fast request? Increase pendingMs or use deferred data loading for non-critical slow work.

keyPoints: Error handling checks the route boundary, then parent boundaries, and finally the router-wide default.
A route's pendingComponent is an optional loading boundary associated with its loader.
The local pending component renders only after the pending threshold is exceeded and only when configured.
The route can override the pending delay with routeOptions.pendingMs.
gotchas: Pending UI is delayed until the configured optimistic threshold, which defaults to one second.
Once displayed, pending UI remains visible for at least the default 500 ms minimum.

Data loading::Preloading on intent.summary: Preloading on intent starts loading a link’s destination when the user focuses, hovers, or touches it. Configure it globally with defaultPreload: 'intent' or per link with preload="intent".
Data loading::Preloading on intent.explanation: Intent preloading attaches to links and starts preparing the destination route when the user focuses, hovers, or touches the link. The router can enable it globally with defaultPreload, while an individual Link can choose its own strategy with preload; focus and hover use a short delay, whereas touch starts immediately.
Data loading::Preloading on intent.syntax:
createRouter({ routeTree, defaultPreload: 'intent', defaultPreloadDelay: 50 })
<Link to="/destination" preload="intent" preloadDelay={50}>Destination</Link>

parameters.name: defaultPreload
parameters.description: Router-wide default strategy; use 'intent' to preload links on user intent.

parameters.name: defaultPreloadDelay
parameters.description: Router-wide delay in milliseconds before focus/hover or viewport preloading.

parameters.name: preload
parameters.description: Per-link preloading strategy that overrides the router default.

parameters.name: preloadDelay
parameters.description: Per-link delay in milliseconds for focus, hover, or viewport preloading.

Data loading::Preloading on intent.returns: The destination route's dependencies are preloaded before navigation; the documentation does not specify a separate return value for the declarative Link configuration.

example.title: Enable intent preloading globally
example.explanation: The router enables intent preloading for links by default, so this link begins preparing the destination when the user shows intent to visit it.

useCases.title: Reduce perceived navigation latency
useCases.scenario: Users commonly move the pointer over or tab to a link before activating it.

useCases.title: Prepare route dependencies
useCases.scenario: A route contains code or loader dependencies that should be ready before the click.

useCases.title: Opt in per destination
useCases.scenario: Only selected links should use proactive loading rather than the whole application.

interview.question: How do you enable intent preloading?
interview.answer: Set defaultPreload to 'intent' in createRouter to enable the strategy for links throughout the application. An individual Link can override that router default with its preload prop.
interview.followUp: How can the delay be changed? Set defaultPreloadDelay on the router globally, or preloadDelay on a specific Link.

interview.question: Which user interactions trigger intent preloading?
interview.answer: Intent preloading responds to focus, hover, and touch interaction on Link components. It preloads the dependencies for the destination route before navigation occurs.
interview.followUp: What happens on touch? Touch intent starts immediately rather than waiting for the focus or hover delay.

interview.question: What timing and cancellation behavior does intent preloading have?
interview.answer: The default delay for focus and hover intent preloading is 50 milliseconds. A pending preload is cancelled when focus or hover ends before the preload begins.
interview.followUp: What independent behavior should be remembered for viewport preloading? Its queued preload is also cancelled if the link leaves the viewport before the delay expires.

keyPoints: The intent strategy prepares a destination from user interaction rather than waiting for navigation.
Set defaultPreload to 'intent' on the router to apply intent preloading to links by default.
A link-level preload value can override the router-wide strategy.
Focus and hover intent uses a 50-millisecond default delay before beginning.
Use router.preloadRoute when preloading must be initiated explicitly rather than by link intent.
gotchas: A focus or hover preload may be cancelled before it starts if the interaction ends.
Touch interaction bypasses the configured preload delay.
Focus and hover preloads do not begin instantly unless the delay is changed.

Data loading::Route loaders.summary: Route loaders fetch a route's asynchronous requirements before its component renders. The router coordinates loaders, exposes their results through route hooks, and can cache or revalidate the data.
Data loading::Route loaders.explanation: A route's loader is an asynchronous data dependency managed by the router. When a match loads, the router runs eligible loaders as part of the loading lifecycle, waits for their results before rendering the route, and exposes the returned value through the route's loader-data hook. Loaders can receive route parameters and other typed dependencies, while the router's caching and revalidation behavior controls when they run again.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: The loader receives the route loader context, including route parameters and dependencies declared for the route.

Data loading::Route loaders.returns: The value returned by the route loader, exposed to the route component as loader data.

example.title: Load route data before rendering
example.explanation: The route loader fetches the post before the route renders, and the component reads the resolved result through the route's typed hook.

useCases.title: Detail pages
useCases.scenario: Fetch a record using a dynamic URL parameter before rendering its detail page.

useCases.title: Nested routes
useCases.scenario: Load shared layout data and child-route data concurrently during navigation.

useCases.title: Fast navigation
useCases.scenario: Preload critical content to avoid component-level loading flashes and request waterfalls.

useCases.title: Cached route data
useCases.scenario: Reuse or refresh previously loaded route data through the router's caching and revalidation lifecycle.

keyPoints: The router invokes a route's loader as its match enters the loading lifecycle.
Eligible route loaders are designed to run in parallel, allowing independent route data to load concurrently.
The component can access the loader's returned value through the corresponding route hook.
Preloading critical render data helps the route appear with required data already available.
Route-level loading avoids serial requests that would otherwise begin only after component rendering.
Data available at render time can make route content more discoverable to search engines.
gotchas: A previously successful match may render its existing loader data immediately while the router refreshes stale data in the background.
Keep critical route data in loaders rather than fetching it only inside components, so navigation avoids loading flashes and request waterfalls.
Read loader output through the route's generated hook instead of duplicating the request in the component.

Data loading::Stale-while-revalidate.sourceTitle: Data Loading | TanStack Router Solid Docs
Data loading::Stale-while-revalidate.summary: TanStack Router can serve cached route-loader data immediately and revalidate stale successful data in the background. Freshness and reload behavior are controlled with staleTime and staleReloadMode.
Data loading::Stale-while-revalidate.explanation: TanStack Router caches route-loader results using a key derived from a route's dependencies. When a matching entry is stale, the router can render its existing loader data immediately and reload the loader in the background; use staleReloadMode: 'blocking' when navigation must wait for the refreshed result.

parameters.name: defaultStaleTime
parameters.description: Router-wide freshness duration for route-loader data, in milliseconds.

parameters.name: defaultStaleReloadMode
parameters.description: Router-wide policy for stale successful loader data: 'background' or 'blocking'.

parameters.name: staleTime
parameters.description: Per-route freshness duration, overriding the router default.

parameters.name: staleReloadMode
parameters.description: Per-route stale reload policy, overriding the router default.

Data loading::Stale-while-revalidate.returns: A route loader's returned data is stored on the route match and may remain available in the in-memory cache after the match becomes inactive.

example.title: Configure background revalidation
example.explanation: Configure a ten-second freshness window and keep stale successful loader data visible while it refreshes.

useCases.title: Refresh without a loading flash
useCases.scenario: A route has cached data that should remain visible while the server request runs again.

useCases.title: Reuse fresh route data
useCases.scenario: A route should avoid repeated loader requests for a defined interval.

useCases.title: Use blocking reloads
useCases.scenario: A route requires the newest loader result before navigation completes.

useCases.title: Cache dependency-specific data
useCases.scenario: A loader depends on route parameters or search values that identify separate results.

interview.question: How does stale-while-revalidate work in TanStack Router?
interview.answer: The router stores loader results in a cache keyed by route dependencies. If reusable data exists, it can be returned immediately; stale successful data is then revalidated in the background by default.
interview.followUp: How would you make navigation wait for fresh data? Set staleReloadMode to 'blocking', which waits for the stale loader reload to finish.

interview.question: What controls whether cached route data is considered fresh?
interview.answer: staleTime controls how long a route match's loader data is fresh. It defaults to routerOptions.defaultStaleTime, whose default is 0 milliseconds.
interview.followUp: What happens when a route is matched again within staleTime? Its loader data remains fresh and is not reloaded.

interview.question: What is the difference between background and blocking stale reloads?
interview.answer: defaultStaleReloadMode controls the default behavior for stale successful loader data. 'background' preserves stale-while-revalidate, while 'blocking' waits for the reload before navigation resolves.
interview.followUp: How can one route override the router default? Set staleReloadMode on that route's options.

keyPoints: Route loaders have built-in stale-while-revalidate caching, so applications do not need a separate cache just for this behavior.
A loader's dependency values determine the cache key for its returned data.
Cached data can render immediately, with background fetching determined by whether the entry is fresh or stale.
The default behavior keeps existing successful data available while the router refreshes it.
Choose background mode for immediate rendering or blocking mode when the stale reload must finish first.
staleTime expresses the freshness duration in milliseconds for a route match's loader result.
gotchas: The default freshness period is zero, so successfully loaded data becomes eligible for revalidation immediately.
Changing the dependencies that form the loader key creates a distinct cache entry; without reusable data, that entry must load.
Set a route's staleTime to Infinity when it should not automatically perform stale reloads.

Hooks::useBlocker.summary: Blocks TanStack Router navigation when a condition is met, such as a dirty form. Use the returned resolver controls to let the user continue or cancel the pending navigation.
Hooks::useBlocker.explanation: useBlocker receives an options object whose shouldBlockFn decides whether the current navigation should stop. With withResolver enabled, the hook exposes status plus proceed and reset controls; enableBeforeUnload separately controls protection for reloads and tab closing.

parameters.name: shouldBlockFn
parameters.description: Required predicate returning whether the current navigation should be blocked; it may return a boolean or Promise<boolean> and receives transition details.

parameters.name: disabled
parameters.description: Disables the blocker entirely; defaults to false.

parameters.name: enableBeforeUnload
parameters.description: Controls browser beforeunload handling; defaults to true. May be a boolean or a function returning one.

parameters.name: withResolver
parameters.description: Uses the resolver returned by the hook for manual resolution; defaults to false.

Hooks::useBlocker.returns: An object containing status ('blocked' or 'idle'), transition details when blocked (next, current, action), and proceed/reset functions for manual resolution.

example.title: Block leaving a dirty editor
example.explanation: Blocks navigation while the editor is dirty; the resolver controls whether the pending navigation continues or is cancelled.

useCases.title: Protect unsaved form data
useCases.scenario: A user edits a form and attempts to navigate away before saving.

useCases.title: Custom confirmation UI
useCases.scenario: An editor should allow navigation only after an application-specific confirmation flow.

useCases.title: Conditional browser unload protection
useCases.scenario: A page needs reload and tab-close protection only while its contents are dirty.

interview.question: What does shouldBlockFn control?
interview.answer: The required shouldBlockFn returns a boolean or Promise<boolean>. Returning true blocks the current navigation, while false allows it.
interview.followUp: How can the decision inspect the transition? Use the function argument, which provides current and next route information plus the navigation action.

interview.question: How do you resolve a blocked navigation?
interview.answer: withResolver enables manual resolution through the hook result. When blocked, proceed continues the navigation and reset cancels it and returns status to idle.
interview.followUp: What state indicates a pending block? The status field is 'blocked'; otherwise it is 'idle'.

interview.question: How does browser unload protection differ from navigation blocking?
interview.answer: enableBeforeUnload controls whether the blocker handles the browser beforeunload event. It accepts a boolean or a function returning a boolean and defaults to true.
interview.followUp: Why might it be set to the dirty state? That limits reload and tab-close protection to periods when unsaved data exists.

keyPoints: Call the hook with one options object rather than positional arguments.
The blocking predicate may make either synchronous or asynchronous decisions.
The predicate receives transition context, including the current route, destination route, and triggering action.
The disabled option is off by default and can turn the blocker off entirely.
Before-unload handling is enabled by default unless configured otherwise.
The hook result provides navigation-blocking controls for resolver-based flows.
gotchas: A false navigation decision does not necessarily prevent the browser's beforeunload event; set enableBeforeUnload explicitly when that behavior must depend on form state.
After a user cancels, pending navigations remain blocked, so provide a clear reset or proceed path.

Hooks::useLinkProps.summary: useLinkProps converts TanStack Router link options and anchor attributes into props for a custom native anchor. It preserves router navigation behavior while letting the component accept standard link features.
Hooks::useLinkProps.explanation: Call useLinkProps with TanStack Router link options plus any supported anchor attributes. It produces the anchor props needed for navigation, including the generated href and router behavior, so a custom component can render a native <a> while retaining router link capabilities such as active-state and preload behavior.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Router link options and React anchor attributes; the documented options type is ActiveLinkOptions & React.AnchorHTMLAttributes<HTMLAnchorElement>.

Hooks::useLinkProps.returns: A React.AnchorHTMLAttributes<HTMLAnchorElement> object that can be applied to an anchor for navigation.

example.title: Custom anchor link
example.explanation: This component forwards navigation options and ordinary anchor attributes to useLinkProps, then applies the returned props to a native anchor.

useCases.scenario: Design-system links

interview.question: What does useLinkProps return?
interview.answer: useLinkProps accepts an options object and returns React.AnchorHTMLAttributes<HTMLAnchorElement>. Apply that result to an anchor to create a navigable custom link.
interview.followUp: How can a custom component retain normal anchor behavior? Pass anchor attributes through the hook's options because it extends React.AnchorHTMLAttributes<HTMLAnchorElement> and merges additional props into the result.

interview.question: What can be supplied to useLinkProps?
interview.answer: Its options combine ActiveLinkOptions with React anchor attributes. This lets the custom component use router navigation options while also accepting standard anchor properties.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful instead of manually building href values? The returned object contains the router-generated link behavior and location details, including pathname, search parameters, hash, and state.

interview.question: How do you build a custom link with the hook?
interview.answer: Render an actual anchor and spread the hook result onto it. The resulting element can navigate to a new location and preserve the link behavior supplied by TanStack Router.
interview.followUp: What router location parts are covered? The hook supports changes to pathname, search params, hash, and location state through its link options.

keyPoints: Call the hook with one options object.
The return value is typed as props for a native HTML anchor.
Spread the returned props onto the custom component's anchor element.
The resulting anchor performs TanStack Router navigation.
Link options can describe pathname, search, hash, and state changes.
The options include active-link behavior through ActiveLinkOptions.
Standard anchor attributes are part of the accepted options type.
gotchas: The hook accepts anchor attributes as well as router options; avoid unintentionally overriding values when spreading or composing the returned object.

Hooks::useLoaderData.sourceTitle: useLoaderData hook | TanStack Router React Docs
Hooks::useLoaderData.summary: Reads loader data from the closest route match after the loader has resolved. Use from for precise route typing, or select to return a derived value and tune re-render behavior.
Hooks::useLoaderData.explanation: useLoaderData reads the resolved loader result associated with a route match. Pass the matching route ID through from for precise typing, or use select to derive a value; the selected value can also control shallow-equality re-render checks.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Route ID of the closest parent match; optional, but recommended for full type safety.

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Whether to enforce strict route typing; defaults to true.

parameters.name: select
parameters.description: Transforms loader data into the value returned by the hook.

parameters.name: structuralSharing
parameters.description: Controls structural sharing for the value returned by select.

Hooks::useLoaderData.returns: With select, returns the selector's value; otherwise returns the loader data, or a loosened version when strict is false.

example.title: Read route loader data
example.explanation: The route loader returns an object, and the route component reads that resolved object with the route-scoped hook.

useCases.title: Render route-loaded data
useCases.scenario: A route component needs the result produced by its own loader.

useCases.title: Consume parent-route data
useCases.scenario: A shared child component needs typed data from a known ancestor route.

useCases.title: Select a focused value
useCases.scenario: A component needs one field or computed slice instead of the entire loader result.

interview.question: What does useLoaderData return?
interview.answer: It returns loader data from the closest RouteMatch in the component tree. With no select function, the result is the loader data, unless strict is false, in which case the type is loosened.
interview.followUp: How can a component consume only part of the loader result? Pass select, which receives the loader data and returns the derived value exposed by the hook.

interview.question: Why use the from option?
interview.answer: The from option is a route ID identifying the closest parent match. It is optional, but recommended for full type safety; when strict is true, TypeScript warns if it is missing.
interview.followUp: What happens when strict is false? The from option is ignored and the returned loader-data type is loosened to cover possible loader data.

interview.question: How does select affect the hook?
interview.answer: select is an optional function shaped like (loaderData: TLoaderData) => TSelected. Its return value becomes the hook result, and TanStack Router uses it for shallow-equality checks when deciding whether the parent component should re-render.
interview.followUp: What related option controls structural sharing for the selected value? structuralSharing configures whether structural sharing is enabled for the value returned by select.

keyPoints: The hook reads data from the nearest matching route available in the component tree.
Configuration is supplied as one options object rather than positional arguments.
from identifies the route whose loader data should be typed and read.
strict defaults to true, preserving the normal strict typing behavior.
select transforms the complete loader result into the value returned by the hook.
structuralSharing controls structural sharing for values produced by select.
gotchas: Omitting from can reduce type precision when strict mode is enabled; provide the closest parent route ID when possible.
Setting strict to false deliberately broadens the returned type and makes from ineffective.
A select function affects re-render behavior, so derive only the data the component needs.

Hooks::useMatch and useMatches.summary: useMatch reads one route match, while useMatches reads the complete presented chain of matches. Use selectors to derive only the data a component needs for breadcrumbs, layouts, or other route-aware UI.
Hooks::useMatch and useMatches.explanation: useMatch reads the RouteMatch identified by from, while useMatches returns the router's complete presented match array regardless of where the component sits in the tree. Both accept select to derive a smaller value and use shallow equality to help control re-renders; useMatch can return undefined when shouldThrow is false and no matching route is present.
Hooks::useMatch and useMatches.syntax:
useMatch({ from, select?, shouldThrow?, structuralSharing? })
useMatches({ select?, structuralSharing? })

parameters.name: opts.from
parameters.description: The route ID of the match to read.

parameters.name: opts.select
parameters.description: Optional selector applied to the single RouteMatch; its result is returned.

parameters.name: opts.select
parameters.description: Optional selector applied to the complete RouteMatch array; its result is returned.

parameters.name: opts.shouldThrow
parameters.description: Whether useMatch throws when the requested match is absent; defaults to true.

parameters.name: opts.structuralSharing
parameters.description: Whether structural sharing is enabled for the value returned by select.

Hooks::useMatch and useMatches.returns: useMatch returns the selected value, or the RouteMatch object when no selector is supplied; with shouldThrow: false, it can return undefined when no match is found. useMatches returns the selected value, or an array of RouteMatch objects when no selector is supplied.

example.title: Read a route match and the full match chain
example.explanation: Reads one known route match safely and derives the complete presented match chain for breadcrumb output.

keyPoints: useMatch reads one RouteMatch associated with the route currently identified by the options.
A RouteMatch exposes the route-match data used by other hooks, including params, loader data, route context, and search.
Pass the target route ID through from; using a specific route ID improves type inference.
useMatches is suited to consumers such as breadcrumbs or layouts that need the entire presented match chain.
Both hooks support select, allowing a component to subscribe to a derived value instead of the entire match object or array.
Selecting a small derived value can reduce unnecessary parent re-renders through shallow-equality comparison.
gotchas: By default, a missing match throws; set shouldThrow to false when the route may not be present, then handle the resulting undefined value.
useMatches is not limited to the caller's local tree position; it returns the complete presented chain, which can include matches below pending, error, or not-found boundaries.
Treat the full array as potentially containing descendants that are still loading, rather than assuming every entry is fully settled.

Hooks::useNavigate.summary: useNavigate returns a typed navigate function for imperative navigation. Use it in event handlers to change the route and optionally provide search parameters, a hash, or location state.
Hooks::useNavigate.explanation: Call useNavigate to obtain a navigate function, optionally anchoring its type context with from. Invoke that function with navigation options such as to, search, hash, or state; it returns a promise that resolves after navigation finishes. Registered route types provide checking for destinations and parameters.

parameters.name: opts.from
parameters.description: Optional route location used as the navigation origin and type context.

parameters.name: navigate options
parameters.description: Navigation configuration, including destination and optional search, hash, or state.

example.title: Navigate from an event handler
example.explanation: Clicking the button imperatively navigates to the posts route with a typed page search parameter.

useCases.title: Navigate after an interaction

useCases.title: Update search parameters
useCases.scenario: A control changes filtering or pagination in the URL.

useCases.title: Pass navigation metadata
useCases.scenario: An action must preserve or set a hash or location state.

A navigation can update the pathname, search parameters, hash, and location state.
Pass one options object to useNavigate; its from value supplies the navigation origin.
Invoke the returned function with one NavigateOptions object.
The navigation call returns a promise that settles after navigation completes.
from identifies the route context used when navigating from a specific location.

Hooks::useParams.summary: Reads typed path parameters from the closest matched route and its parent matches. Use from for route-specific typing, select for a derived result, or strict: false when the location is ambiguous.
Hooks::useParams.explanation: useParams reads path parameters from the nearest route match and its parent matches. Provide from to target a route precisely, select to return a derived value, or strict: false when the calling location is ambiguous; the result is inferred from the registered route types.
Hooks::useParams.syntax: useParams<TSelected = TAllParams>(opts?: { from?: string; strict?: boolean; select?: (params: TAllParams) => TSelected }): TSelected

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Optional route and selection settings. Common fields are from, strict, and select.

parameters.name: opts.from
parameters.description: Route path used to identify the match whose parameter types should be read; ignored when strict is false.

parameters.name: opts.strict
parameters.description: When false, permits ambiguous usage and loosens the result to Partial<AllParams>. Defaults to true.

parameters.name: opts.select
parameters.description: Receives the parameter object and determines the hook's returned value.

Hooks::useParams.returns: An object containing the matched route's and parent matches' path parameters, or TSelected when select is provided.

interview.question: What does useParams return?
interview.answer: useParams returns the path parameters from the closest match together with parameters from its parent matches. Its result is an object unless select is supplied, in which case it is the selector's return value.
interview.followUp: How can a component read parameters from an ambiguous location? Use strict: false, accepting the loosened Partial<AllParams> type.

interview.question: How do from and select affect useParams?
interview.answer: The from option identifies the route whose parameter types should be used. The select callback receives the parameter object and lets the hook return a narrower or derived value.
interview.followUp: Why might select be preferable to destructuring in the component? It lets the hook return only the needed value and supports a focused subscription result.

interview.question: What is the effect of strict: false?
interview.answer: By default, strict is true. With strict: false, from is ignored and the result uses Partial<AllParams>, reflecting parameters shared across possible matches.
interview.followUp: What trade-off comes with strict: false? The component can be used from an ambiguous location, but TypeScript can no longer guarantee that every parameter exists.

keyPoints: The hook combines parameters from the closest matched route and every parent match.
Options control route targeting, strictness, and result selection.
select transforms the full parameter object into the value returned by the hook.
Without select the result is the parameter object; with select it is TSelected.
gotchas: Setting strict to false ignores from and weakens the result to Partial<AllParams>, so parameter properties may be absent.
Calling the hook without options is supported, but route-specific typing and selection require the options object.

Hooks::useRouteContext.explanation: Call the hook inside a component with an options object identifying the route through from. It returns that route's context; when select is supplied, it applies the function to the context and returns the selected value instead.

parameters.name: opts.from
parameters.description: Required route identifier used to select the route context.

parameters.name: opts.select
parameters.description: Optional function receiving the route context and returning the value exposed by the hook.

Hooks::useRouteContext.returns: The current route context, or TSelected when a select function is supplied.

interview.question: What does useRouteContext do?
interview.answer: useRouteContext is a hook for obtaining the context belonging to the current route in a component. Its options object requires from, which identifies the route whose context is requested.
interview.followUp: How can a component avoid consuming the entire context? Pass select and return only the needed property; the hook then returns that selected value.

interview.question: What is the purpose of from?
interview.answer: The from option is a string RouteID and is required. It tells TanStack Router which route context to match.
interview.followUp: What happens if from is omitted? The documented hook signature requires it, so the call is not a valid documented usage.

interview.question: How does select change the hook's result?
interview.answer: select is optional and receives the route-context object. The hook returns the callback's result instead of the full context when select is provided.
interview.followUp: What type does the hook return with select? It returns the selected value, such as a string when the callback selects a string property.

keyPoints: It reads the context associated with the route currently represented by the component.
Use it from a component that needs values supplied through route context.
The call is configured with an object rather than a positional route argument.
The optional selector receives the route context and can produce a different result type.
Its return value is either the complete context or the selector's output.
gotchas: The from option is required, so the hook must identify which route's context it should read.
A select callback changes the result from the complete context to whatever value the callback returns.

Hooks::useRouter.summary: useRouter returns the current TanStack Router instance from context. Use it for imperative router work such as invalidation, while useRouterState is required for reactive router-state rendering.
Hooks::useRouter.explanation: In a component, useRouter retrieves the current Router instance from context. The returned instance provides imperative APIs such as invalidate; its state can be read directly, but reading router.state does not subscribe the component to updates. Use useRouterState when rendered output must react to router-state changes.
Hooks::useRouter.returns: The current Router instance from context.

useCases.title: Invalidate route data
useCases.scenario: A user action should refresh route loader data after a mutation.

useCases.title: Perform an imperative route match

useCases.title: Access router operations
useCases.scenario: A component needs direct access to router APIs exposed by the current application router.

interview.question: What does useRouter return?
interview.answer: useRouter returns the current Router instance from context. It is intended for accessing the router from a component and performing imperative operations.
interview.followUp: How should a component reactively render from router state? Use useRouterState rather than reading router.state directly, because direct state access is not reactive.

interview.question: Give one practical use of the router returned by useRouter.
interview.answer: The hook returns the router instance, which can be used for imperative APIs such as invalidation. For example, an event handler can call router.invalidate().
interview.followUp: When should matching be performed imperatively? In an event handler, use the router instance and call router.matchRoute rather than subscribing through a matching hook.

interview.question: Where does useRouter obtain the router instance?
interview.answer: useRouter reads the router from context, so it is used inside a component rendered within the router's context. The returned Router instance is the current application router.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies to the router instance's state? router.state stays current but does not itself establish a reactive subscription.

keyPoints: useRouter obtains the current Router instance through context.
Use it in components that need to call router APIs directly.
The instance exposes current state, but reading that state alone does not subscribe the component.
Choose useRouterState when rendered UI must update as router state changes.
gotchas: Reading router.state gives current data but does not cause the component to re-render when that state changes.
Use useRouterState instead when the component needs router-state changes to trigger rendering.

Hooks::useRouterState.summary: A hook for reactively reading TanStack Router's current internal state. Use select to subscribe to a derived value such as location or navigation status.
Hooks::useRouterState.explanation: Call the hook inside a router-connected component to subscribe to router state. Without options it returns the complete RouterState; supplying select derives a narrower value such as location or status, and structuralSharing can control reference reuse for that selected result.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Optional configuration object for selecting a value and configuring structural sharing.

parameters.name: opts.select
parameters.description: Optional function called with RouterState; its result becomes the hook result.

parameters.name: opts.structuralSharing
parameters.description: Optional setting controlling structural sharing for the selected value.

Hooks::useRouterState.returns: The current RouterState object, or TSelected when select is provided.

example.title: Read the router status
example.explanation: Selects the router's status so the component renders the current navigation state.

useCases.title: Navigation progress UI
useCases.scenario: Render a global loading indicator while navigation is pending.

useCases.title: Reactive router data
useCases.scenario: Read a selected location or status value in a component that must update reactively.

useCases.title: Fine-grained state subscription
useCases.scenario: Subscribe to a focused slice of router state to limit unnecessary component updates.

interview.question: What does useRouterState return?
interview.answer: useRouterState is a hook that returns the router's current internal state. With no options, its result is a RouterState object.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid subscribing to more state than necessary? Use select to return only the value the component needs.

interview.question: How do you select a derived router value?
interview.answer: Pass an options object with select, a function receiving RouterState and returning the selected value. The hook then returns that selected value instead of the whole state.
interview.followUp: What additional option affects selected results? structuralSharing configures whether structural sharing is enabled for the value returned by select.

interview.question: Why use this hook instead of router.state?
interview.answer: It provides reactive router-state access for components, unlike directly reading router.state. A component using router.state does not re-render when router state changes.
interview.followUp: Which specialized hooks should be considered for common data? useLocation and useMatches are preferred for current location and matches.

keyPoints: It exposes the router's internal state through a component hook.
The argument is optional, so the complete state can be read without configuration.
select receives RouterState and produces a selected value with type TSelected.
The hook returns the result of select rather than the original state when a selector is provided.
The return type depends on whether select is present.
gotchas: Prefer useLocation or useMatches for location or match data; they are intended to be more ergonomic and performant than reading the entire router state.
Do not substitute router.state for this hook in a component when updates should trigger a re-render.

Hooks::useSearch.summary: useSearch reads the current location’s validated search parameters as a typed object. It can scope types to a route, select a derived value, or use looser shared-search typing.
Hooks::useSearch.explanation: useSearch accepts an options object and returns the current location’s search parameters as an object. Provide a route ID or path with from for route-specific type inference, optionally transform the result with select, or set strict to false when accessing shared search parameters without a route origin.

parameters.name: opts.from
parameters.description: Route ID or path used to match the search parameters. Required for strict route-specific usage.

parameters.name: opts.shouldThrow
parameters.description: Whether missing route context should throw; defaults to true.

parameters.name: opts.select
parameters.description: Transforms the search object; the selected return value becomes the hook result.

parameters.name: opts.structuralSharing
parameters.description: Controls structural sharing for the selected result.

parameters.name: opts.strict
parameters.description: When false, ignores from and loosens the result to Partial<FullSearchSchema>; defaults to true.

Hooks::useSearch.returns: With from, returns the current location’s search parameters for that route, or TSelected when select is supplied. With strict: false, returns the current search parameters typed as Partial<FullSearchSchema>, or TSelected when select is supplied.

example.title: Read typed search parameters
example.explanation: Reads the validated search object for the /products route and renders it.

useCases.title: Read route search state
useCases.scenario: A route component needs validated filters, pagination, or sorting from the URL.

useCases.title: Select a focused value
useCases.scenario: A component depends on one search field or a computed projection.

useCases.title: Access shared search state
useCases.scenario: A shared component reads search parameters without a known route origin.

interview.question: What does useSearch return, and why use from?
interview.answer: useSearch returns the current location's search query parameters as an object. Passing from identifies the route whose search schema should provide the types.
interview.followUp: How can a component subscribe to only one search value? Use select, for example select: search => search.filter, so the hook returns only that selected value.

interview.question: How does select change useSearch?
interview.answer: select receives the search object and its return value becomes the hook result. This lets a component read a derived value or a narrow subset instead of the entire search object.
interview.followUp: What additional option can preserve references for selected JSON-compatible results? Enable structuralSharing in the hook options.

interview.question: What is the effect of strict: false?
interview.answer: By default strict is true. With strict false, from is ignored and the result is typed as Partial<FullSearchSchema>, reflecting shared search parameters across routes.
interview.followUp: When should strict remain enabled? Keep it enabled when the component has a known route origin and should receive the strongest route-specific types.

keyPoints: The hook exposes the current location’s search state as an object rather than requiring manual query-string parsing.
Configuration is supplied through one options object.
Use from to anchor inference to a particular route ID or path.
select can project the full search object into a value tailored to the component.
structuralSharing controls reference reuse for values produced by select.
strict defaults to true, keeping route-aware typing as the normal behavior.
gotchas: Setting strict to false ignores from and loosens the result to a partial full search schema, reducing route-specific type safety.

Production concerns::Devtools.summary: TanStack Router Devtools visualize the router's internal behavior during development. Install the separate package and mount the component in a root route for automatic connection, or pass the router explicitly when rendering it elsewhere.
Production concerns::Devtools.explanation: TanStack Router Devtools provide a live view of the router's internal behavior. Install the separate package, then render the devtools in a root route; this automatically connects them to the router, while passing an explicit router instance is an alternative when rendering elsewhere.

parameters.name: router
parameters.description: The router instance to inspect when the devtools are not rendered within the router's route tree.

Production concerns::Devtools.returns: A React devtools component that renders an inspector for TanStack Router's runtime state.

example.title: Mount TanStack Router Devtools
example.explanation: Mount the devtools in the root route so they connect automatically to the router and expose its runtime state.

useCases.title: Inspect router behavior
useCases.scenario: Debugging a navigation whose route matching or loading behavior is unexpected.

useCases.title: Monitor route state
useCases.scenario: Adding a development-only inspector to an application root.

useCases.title: Connect an external mount
useCases.scenario: Using a custom application shell where the devtools cannot live inside a route.

interview.question: How do you add TanStack Router Devtools to a React application?
interview.answer: The devtools are installed separately and rendered with TanStackRouterDevtools. Placing them inside the root route automatically connects them to the router instance.
interview.followUp: How would you mount them outside a route? Pass the same router instance used by RouterProvider through the devtools' router prop.

interview.question: Where should the devtools component be rendered?
interview.answer: Render TanStackRouterDevtools in a root or other route, typically alongside Outlet. The component then has access to the router and can show its runtime behavior for debugging.
interview.followUp: What setup avoids relying on route context? Render the component next to RouterProvider and provide router explicitly.

interview.question: How can you configure the devtools outside the route tree?
interview.answer: When the component is not rendered inside RouterProvider's route tree, give it the router instance through its router prop. That instance should be the same one passed to RouterProvider.
interview.followUp: Why must the instances match? The devtools need the active router's state rather than a separately created router with unrelated navigation state.

keyPoints: Use the panel to inspect the router's internal runtime behavior while diagnosing navigation.
Mounting in the root route is the recommended integration point.
The component can also be rendered from another route when that placement suits the application.
When mounted outside the route tree, configure the component with the router instance used by the application.
gotchas: Install the dedicated devtools package before importing or rendering the component.
Rendering inside a route is the simplest setup; placing the component elsewhere requires explicitly supplying the router.

Production concerns::Lazy routes.summary: Lazy routes keep non-critical route code out of the initial bundle and load it when its route is visited. TanStack Router supports automatic splitting, .lazy.tsx files, and Route.lazy() for code-based routing.
Production concerns::Lazy routes.explanation: Lazy routes separate non-critical route pieces from the configuration needed to match a URL and begin loading data. The bundler can create separate chunks for components and other supported properties, then resolve those pieces on demand when the route loads. File-based projects can use automatic splitting or a .lazy.tsx file; code-based projects can attach a lazy importer with Route.lazy().

parameters.name: lazyImporter
parameters.description: A function returning a promise of partial route options that are applied when the route is loaded lazily.

Production concerns::Lazy routes.returns: Route instance (this) from Route.lazy; lazy route components return a component that can be preloaded.

example.title: Automatically split a file-based route
example.explanation: With the bundler plugin configured for automatic splitting, the route component is emitted into a separate chunk and fetched when this route is loaded.

useCases.title: Reduce the initial JavaScript bundle
useCases.scenario: Large file-based application

useCases.title: Enable automatic route chunking
useCases.scenario: Projects using the bundler plugin

useCases.title: Split a route with .lazy.tsx
useCases.scenario: Manual file-based setup

useCases.title: Attach a deferred route definition with Route.lazy()
useCases.scenario: Code-based routing

interview.question: How do you enable automatic lazy route splitting?
interview.answer: Automatic code splitting is enabled with autoCodeSplitting: true in the TanStack Router bundler plugin. The plugin transforms route files so supported properties can be placed in separate lazy-loaded chunks.
interview.followUp: Which route properties can be split? The documented properties are component, errorComponent, pendingComponent, notFoundComponent, and loader.

interview.question: How can file-based routing split a route when automatic splitting is unavailable?
interview.answer: For file-based routing, put non-critical route code in a file ending with .lazy.tsx and use createLazyFileRoute instead of createFileRoute. The normal route file retains the critical configuration.
interview.followUp: What is the code-based equivalent? Create a lazy route with createLazyRoute, then attach it through the route definition's lazy method.

interview.question: What does Route.lazy accept and when is it resolved?
interview.answer: The Route.lazy method accepts a function returning a promise of partial updatable route options: (lazyImporter: () => Promise<Partial<UpdatableRouteOptions>>) => this. The importer is resolved lazily while the route loads.
interview.followUp: How can chunk grouping be customized? Use codeSplitGroupings to place selected supported properties into the same generated bundle.

keyPoints: Critical configuration stays in the eagerly available route definition so matching and initial data loading can start without waiting for the lazy chunk.
Components and other non-critical configuration can be deferred because they are unnecessary for identifying the route.
The manual file-based approach places lazy route implementation in a companion .lazy.tsx file.
Code-based routes connect their deferred implementation by calling lazy on the route definition.
Fine-grained grouping controls which supported route properties share a generated chunk.
gotchas: Do not export split properties such as component or loader from the route file, because exporting them prevents code splitting.

Production concerns::Route guards.summary: Use beforeLoad on a route, commonly a protected layout, to check authentication or roles and throw redirect() when access is denied. Treat this as route/UI control only; private data needs authorization in its server or API handler.
Production concerns::Route guards.explanation: A route's beforeLoad runs before the route loads and can inspect authentication or authorization data from context. If the check fails, throw redirect() to stop navigation and send the user to login or an unauthorized page; preserve location.href when returning the user afterward. Apply checks on parent layout routes to protect their descendants, but authorize private data separately in every server function, server route, or API endpoint.

parameters.name: beforeLoad arguments
parameters.description: Object passed to beforeLoad; examples use context for auth state and location for the current URL.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Authentication and authorization state exposed through the router context.

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: The current route location, including href for preserving the requested destination.

Production concerns::Route guards.returns: A beforeLoad guard may return route context data or throw redirect() to interrupt navigation; the cited examples use redirects for failed checks.

example.title: Protect an admin route subtree
example.explanation: A layout route checks the authenticated user's role before its protected subtree loads and sends unauthorized users to an error page while preserving the intended location.

useCases.title: Redirect unauthenticated users
useCases.scenario: A visitor opens a private route without a valid session.

useCases.title: Enforce role-based UI access
useCases.scenario: A signed-in user lacks the role required by an administrative subtree.

useCases.title: Guard permission-specific screens
useCases.scenario: A user lacks one or more permissions needed by a route.

useCases.title: Preserve the post-login destination
useCases.scenario: A login flow should return the user to the page they originally requested.

interview.question: How do you implement an authentication guard?
interview.answer: beforeLoad runs before a route is loaded and receives the same arguments as the route loader. Use it to inspect authentication or roles, then throw redirect() when access should be denied.
interview.followUp: Where should the actual data authorization happen? Every server function, server route, or API endpoint that reads or writes private data must authorize the request independently.

interview.question: How would you protect an admin route subtree?
interview.answer: Put the guard on a parent layout route so its child routes inherit the protection. A failed role check can throw redirect({ to: '/unauthorized' }) and include the current location in search parameters.
interview.followUp: How can several routes share an authorization rule? Create a protected layout route for the subtree and perform the shared check in that layout's beforeLoad.

interview.question: How do you preserve the intended destination after login?
interview.answer: Use the location argument supplied to beforeLoad and save location.href in the redirect search parameters. After authentication, that value can guide navigation back to the originally requested page.
interview.followUp: What location value should be avoided for this purpose? router.state.resolvedLocation may lag behind the actual current location, so it should not be used.

keyPoints: beforeLoad is the route-level hook for running authentication and authorization checks before loading the route.
Unauthenticated users can be redirected to a login route instead of entering the protected screen.
Navigation is redirected by throwing redirect() from the guard, rather than merely returning a redirect object.
Route guards control navigation and UI; private data still requires authorization at its server/API boundary.
gotchas: Do not treat beforeLoad as the security boundary: independently authorize every server function, server route, or API endpoint that accesses private data.
When storing a return destination, use location.href from beforeLoad rather than router.state.resolvedLocation.

Production concerns::Router context.explanation: Define the root context type with createRootRouteWithContext, then provide matching dependency values through createRouter's context option. Matching routes receive inherited context, and a route can extend or change it with beforeLoad for its descendants.

parameters.name: context

useCases.scenario: Provide a QueryClient, API client, or mutation service to loaders without importing it in every route.

useCases.title: Authentication context
useCases.scenario: Make authentication or session state available to route guards and descendant loaders.

useCases.title: Hierarchical route dependencies
useCases.scenario: Add route-specific values in beforeLoad for nested routes.

interview.question: What is router context used for?
interview.answer: Router context is a typed dependency-injection mechanism that flows through the router and matching route hierarchy. A route can read it in APIs such as beforeLoad and loader without importing or constructing the dependency itself.
interview.followUp: How would you make a required dependency type-safe? Use createRootRouteWithContext<ContextType>(), then pass an object satisfying that type in createRouter({ context }).

interview.question: How do you supply a shared client or session?
interview.answer: Create a root route with createRootRouteWithContext and provide the resulting context object through the router's context option. Child routes inherit the values from their matched parents.
interview.followUp: What happens when a route changes context? Its beforeLoad result is merged into the route match tree, making the added or changed values available to descendants.

interview.question: How does context behave across nested routes?
interview.answer: Context is hierarchical: the router supplies initial values, and each route may add to or modify them. Loaders and other route APIs receive the resulting context for their position in the tree.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for authentication? A parent route can establish authentication-related context before descendants load, so those descendants can use the inherited value.

keyPoints: Initial context travels only through routes that participate in the current match.
Routes can extend or replace inherited values for the portion of the tree below them.
Use context to inject reusable services instead of importing or constructing them inside route code.
beforeLoad can contribute route-specific context, and that contribution is merged for descendant routes.
The initial dependency object is supplied in createRouter when the router is instantiated.
Typed route definitions can consume context, including in loader functions.
gotchas: Using createRootRoute alone does not constrain the root context type; use createRootRouteWithContext with the context interface.
Dependencies must be available when the router is created rather than being supplied later during navigation.

Production concerns::Scroll restoration.explanation: Set scrollRestoration to true when creating the router. TanStack Router monitors scroll events, records positions for registered scrollable areas—including the window and body—and restores them at the appropriate navigation point before the browser paints. Use resetScroll when an individual navigation should opt out.

parameters.name: scrollRestorationBehavior
