interview.question: How does TanStack Router restore scroll positions?
interview.answer: Enable scrollRestoration in the router configuration. The router then observes scroll activity, caches positions for scrollable areas, and restores them around router navigation rather than requiring application-level browser-history handling.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the position of a virtualized element? Use useElementScrollRestoration with a unique id and the data-scroll-restoration-id attribute, then provide the returned scroll position to the virtualizer.

interview.question: How can one navigation opt out of scroll handling?
interview.answer: Set resetScroll to false on a Link, navigate call, or redirect call. That suppresses restoration for the next navigation when returning to an existing history event, and suppresses the top reset for a new history event.
interview.followUp: How can navigation use a different cache identity? Configure getKey so the cache associates positions with the location identity your application needs instead of the default history-entry key.

interview.question: Which built-in scroll behaviors and controls are available?
interview.answer: The router supports hash scrolling and top-of-page scrolling without extra configuration. For transitions, scrollRestorationBehavior accepts browser-style smooth, instant, or auto behavior.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when a nested scrolling container is not restored? Register the element with the restoration mechanism and give it a stable data-scroll-restoration-id for manual control.

keyPoints: Hash targets and ordinary top-of-page movement work by default, so basic routes need no separate scroll setup.
The restoration system watches DOM scroll events to keep its position data current.
Scrollable elements must be registered with the cache so the router can track more than the main document.
The cache stores positions independently for each scrollable area, including window and body.
Restoration occurs after a successful navigation and before DOM painting, helping avoid a visible jump.
Use the element hook when an individual scroll container needs application-controlled restoration.
gotchas: Setting resetScroll to false skips restoration for the next navigation; on a new history entry it also prevents the normal reset to the top.
The default cache key uses TanStack Router's unique history-entry key, so changing key generation changes which navigations share stored positions.

Production concerns::Server-side renderi.summary: TanStack Router renders the matched route on the server and hydrates the resulting HTML in the browser. Route loader data is automatically dehydrated and rehydrated when the standard SSR setup is used.
Production concerns::Server-side renderi.explanation: TanStack Router supports SSR by rendering the matched application route on the server and sending HTML plus the serialized state needed by the browser. The client then uses RouterClient to hydrate that existing markup, while resolved loader data is automatically dehydrated and rehydrated when the standard SSR setup is followed.
Production concerns::Server-side renderi.returns: Server-rendered HTML for the matched route; client hydration produces a fully interactive application.

example.title: Render and hydrate a matched route
example.explanation: The server renders the router's matched route into HTML, while the browser hydrates that output through RouterClient.

useCases.title: Non-streaming SSR
useCases.scenario: Deliver complete HTML for a route in one response before client JavaScript runs.

useCases.title: Streaming SSR
useCases.scenario: Send the initial route content progressively as server rendering continues.

useCases.title: Loader-data hydration
useCases.scenario: Reuse resolved route loader data during hydration instead of loading it again.

keyPoints: SSR creates the initial route HTML on the server and sends it to the browser.
Hydration attaches client behavior to the HTML instead of requiring a second document render.
Non-streaming SSR returns the complete page in one response.
Streaming SSR can send the critical first paint while the server continues producing the rest.
Route loader results can cross the server-client boundary automatically when the documented SSR steps are complete.
The client-side SSR entry uses RouterClient to hydrate the router output.
gotchas: Hydration requires the client output to correspond to the server-rendered markup; mismatches can prevent correct interactivity.
For streaming SSR, the root route must render Scripts inside body so route scripts and streamed hydration data can be inserted.

Routing fundamentals::Code-based routing.sourceTitle: Code-Based Routing | TanStack Router Solid Docs
Routing fundamentals::Code-based routing.summary: Code-based routing declares TanStack Router routes directly in code and assembles them into an explicit nested route tree. It is useful when route structure is dynamic or shared, though the documentation recommends file-based routing for most applications.
Routing fundamentals::Code-based routing.explanation: Code-based routing declares TanStack Router routes with route APIs, then explicitly connects them into a nested route tree passed to the router. Each non-root route normally supplies a path; dynamic segments beginning with `$` become route parameters.

parameters.name: getParentRoute
parameters.description: The parent route accessor used by a child route to identify its place in the route hierarchy.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: The URL pattern used for matching; required for routes other than the root or a pathless layout route.

parameters.name: routeTree
parameters.description: The final nested route tree supplied when creating the router.

Routing fundamentals::Code-based routing.returns: A configured router created from the explicitly assembled route tree.

example.title: Explicit code-based route tree
example.explanation: This constructs a root route, declares child routes in code, assembles the route tree, and creates the router.

useCases.title: Dynamic route structures
useCases.scenario: The route hierarchy is generated or varies at runtime or build time.

useCases.title: Shared route configuration
useCases.scenario: Several routes or route definitions need to be shared through ordinary code modules.

useCases.title: Explicit route-tree assembly
useCases.scenario: A project needs direct control over how route definitions are composed into one tree.

keyPoints: Routes are organized through TypeScript or JavaScript declarations instead of a filesystem route structure.
Code-based and file-based routing share the same nested route-tree model and matching behavior.
Use `createRoute` for ordinary routes and `createRootRoute` for the root route.
Ordinary URL-matching routes require a `path` option; root and pathless layout routes are exceptions.
A route’s `path` determines whether its pattern matches the URL pathname.
Prefix a path segment with `$` to capture its value in the route parameters.
gotchas: Defining a route's parent does not automatically include the route in the final tree; add each route to its parent’s children array.
Use `/` for an index route in code-based routing rather than an index filename convention.
The documentation recommends file-based routing for most applications, so choose code-based routing deliberately.

Routing fundamentals::File-based routing.summary: File-based routing derives TanStack Router's route tree from files and directories. The filesystem layout exposes URL nesting, while the Router plugin or CLI generates the route configuration.
Routing fundamentals::File-based routing.explanation: TanStack Router can derive an application's nested route structure from files and directories rather than requiring the structure to be written entirely in code. A supported bundler plugin or the Router CLI scans the route directory and generates the route configuration, so moving or adding route files keeps the URL structure visible in the project layout.

example.title: A file-backed route
example.explanation: The file location represents the route hierarchy, while the generated route tree supplies the router with the resulting configuration.

useCases.title: Filesystem-visible routes
useCases.scenario: Organize a growing application by URL hierarchy.

useCases.title: Generated route configuration
useCases.scenario: Avoid hand-maintaining route-tree declarations.

useCases.title: Flat route conventions
useCases.scenario: Represent nesting without deeply nested folders.

interview.question: How does TanStack Router implement file-based routing?
interview.answer: File-based routing represents route hierarchy with files and directories. The TanStack Router plugin or CLI then generates the route configuration during development and builds.
interview.followUp: What happens after a route file is moved? The generated route tree is regenerated, reflecting the new filesystem-based hierarchy.

interview.question: How do files and directories map to route hierarchy?
interview.answer: Directories represent nested route levels, and a dot in a filename can represent nesting in flat-route conventions. This lets the URL structure remain discoverable from the route directory.
interview.followUp: When would flat routes be useful? They can express nesting without creating nested directories, while retaining filename-based route discovery.

interview.question: What setup is required to enable file-based routing?
interview.answer: A project must configure either the TanStack Router plugin or the TanStack Router CLI. With a supported bundler, the plugin automatically generates the route configuration in development and build processes.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off with code-based routing? Code-based routing gives explicit route declarations, whereas file-based routing generally reduces the amount of route-structure code.

keyPoints: Routes are configured from the filesystem instead of requiring the complete route hierarchy to be declared directly in application code.
A route file or directory placement communicates its position in the nested route hierarchy.
In flat-route naming, a dot in a filename expresses another nesting level.
Flat routing is an alternative convention that encodes nesting levels in filenames.
Enable the feature by configuring the bundler plugin or the Router CLI.
The bundler integration regenerates route configuration during development and production builds.
gotchas: File-based routing requires React with a supported bundler when using the documented setup.
The automatic generation behavior depends on using one of the supported bundler integrations.

Routing fundamentals::Layout and pathles.summary: Layout routes wrap child routes with shared UI or logic. Prefixing a file-based layout with `_` makes it pathless, so it contributes no URL segment while its children still render within the shared route tree.
Routing fundamentals::Layout and pathles.explanation: A layout route wraps its children with shared UI or route logic. In file-based routing, prefixing the route filename with `_` makes it pathless, so the route participates in nesting while contributing no URL segment; the text after `_` still identifies the route. Its children render through the layout's `Outlet`.

example.title: A pathless layout
example.explanation: The `_app` file creates a pathless layout; child routes render inside its `Outlet` without adding `app` to their URLs.

useCases.title: Shared application chrome
useCases.scenario: Several pages need the same navigation, shell, or visual wrapper while retaining distinct URLs.

useCases.title: Shared access and loading logic
useCases.scenario: A group of routes must pass an authentication or loader check before rendering.

useCases.title: Shared route data and context
useCases.scenario: Descendants need common search-parameter validation or route context.

interview.question: What distinguishes a pathless layout route from an ordinary layout route?
interview.answer: A layout route wraps child routes with shared components or logic. A pathless layout does the same without requiring a matching URL segment, and file-based pathless layouts use an `_` prefix.
interview.followUp: How would you create one in code-based routing? Use a route with an `id` and no `path`; the filesystem `_` convention is unnecessary there.

interview.question: How is a pathless layout represented in file-based routing?
interview.answer: The underscore prefix marks a file-based route as pathless. Its children still inherit the wrapper, but matching their URLs does not include that prefix or the identifier after it.
interview.followUp: What does the text after the underscore do? It forms the route ID, which uniquely identifies the route and supports TypeScript inference and autocomplete.

interview.question: When would you choose a pathless layout?
interview.answer: Pathless layouts are useful when several routes need common UI or behavior without sharing a URL segment. Examples include shared navigation, authentication checks, search-parameter handling, loaders, error fallbacks, pending elements, and context.
interview.followUp: Can a pathless layout use a dynamic segment? No. Because it is not matched by URL segments, dynamic segments cannot be part of its path.

keyPoints: Use a layout route to apply shared presentation or behavior to every nested child.
A pathless layout adds nesting and composition without adding a pathname segment.
In file-based routing, begin the route filename with `_` to declare it pathless.
The suffix after `_` supplies the route ID, so choose a unique descriptive name.
Layouts can validate search parameters and make them available to descendants.
A layout can expose shared context for all of its child routes.
gotchas: The name after `_` is not discarded: it supplies the route ID, which must remain unique.

Routing fundamentals::Not-found and erro.sourceTitle: Not Found Errors | TanStack Router Docs
Routing fundamentals::Not-found and erro.summary: Configure notFoundComponent for missing matches and missing resources, and errorComponent for route failures. Fuzzy mode uses the nearest suitable not-found boundary; root mode sends all not-found errors to the root.
Routing fundamentals::Not-found and erro.explanation: TanStack Router handles missing matches with notFoundComponent and runtime route failures with errorComponent. A route can provide either boundary, while router defaults supply fallbacks; fuzzy mode chooses the nearest suitable not-found boundary and root mode always uses the root one.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration for the notFound function, including routing behavior such as routeId and whether to throw the result.

Routing fundamentals::Not-found and erro.returns: The notFound function returns a NotFoundError object; with throw: true it throws that object instead.

example.title: Route-level not-found and error handling
example.explanation: The root supplies global not-found and error boundaries, while the post loader raises a not-found result when its data is absent.

useCases.title: Render a 404 boundary
useCases.scenario: A URL matches no route or contains unmatched trailing segments.

useCases.title: Report a missing resource
useCases.scenario: A loader cannot find the entity identified by route parameters.

useCases.title: Use fuzzy branch-level handling
useCases.scenario: Different route branches need distinct missing-page experiences.

useCases.title: Centralize not-found handling
useCases.scenario: The application requires one consistent 404 screen.

interview.question: How do not-found and ordinary errors differ?
interview.answer: Use notFoundComponent for a missing route or an explicitly missing resource, and errorComponent for an error encountered by a route. The corresponding route option determines the rendered boundary.
interview.followUp: How can a loader mark a resource as missing? Throw the object returned by notFound(), optionally supplying routeId when the not-found result should be handled at a chosen route.

interview.question: How does notFoundMode affect boundary selection?
interview.answer: The default not-found mode is fuzzy: TanStack Router searches for the nearest matching route that has a suitable notFoundComponent. With root mode, the root route handles every not-found error.
interview.followUp: When would root mode be preferable? Use it when the application requires one consistent global 404 experience rather than branch-specific handling.

interview.question: What configuration provides fallback boundaries?
interview.answer: A route-level notFoundComponent handles not-found errors for that route, while defaultNotFoundComponent provides a router-wide fallback. If no suitable route handles the error, the root route ultimately renders the fallback behavior.
interview.followUp: What happens if a route has no errorComponent? Its error handling uses the router's defaultErrorComponent unless a more specific configured boundary applies.

keyPoints: Unknown paths are converted into not-found errors automatically, including paths with extra unmatched segments.
Configure a route boundary or a router default to replace the basic fallback experience.
Fuzzy mode selects the closest suitable boundary in the matched branch.
Root mode centralizes all not-found rendering at the root.
A route boundary can handle both unmatched paths and not-found results thrown during route processing.
notFoundComponent renders after a not-found error reaches the route responsible for handling it.
gotchas: Do not build new implementations around NotFoundRoute; use notFoundComponent instead.
A missing boundary eventually falls back to the root route's default not-found handling.
The older NotFoundRoute API is deprecated.

Routing fundamentals::Path parameters.summary: Define named URL segments with `$`, then read their inferred values from route params without casting. Parameters are available in loaders and route components, while the global hook supports access from ambiguous component locations.
Routing fundamentals::Path parameters.explanation: Prefix a route segment with `$` and give it a name, such as `$postId`. TanStack Router captures the matching URL segment and exposes it through the route’s typed params, including in loaders and components. For an ambiguous component location, the global `useParams` hook can read params with `strict: false`.

parameters.name: path parameter
parameters.description: The named dynamic segment in the route path, such as `$postId`; its value is parsed from the matching URL segment.

Routing fundamentals::Path parameters.returns: A typed params object whose properties correspond to the named dynamic segments in the route.

example.title: Read a typed path parameter
example.explanation: The route declares a named dynamic segment, and the generated route hook returns its typed value.

useCases.title: Resource detail routes
useCases.scenario: A detail page such as `/posts/123` needs the post identifier to load and render the matching record.

useCases.title: Loader-driven data fetching
useCases.scenario: A loader needs a route identifier to fetch data before the component renders.

useCases.title: Cross-route parameter access
useCases.scenario: A shared component needs access to the matched parameters without being bound to one route.

useCases.title: Optional route segments
useCases.scenario: A route should accept a URL segment only when it is present.

interview.question: How do you define a path parameter in TanStack Router?
interview.answer: A dynamic path segment starts with `$` and names the parameter, for example `/posts/$postId`. The matched value is available as `postId` in the route params and is inferred by the router.
interview.followUp: How would you access a parameter from a component that is not tied to one route? Use the globally exported `useParams` hook with `strict: false`.

interview.question: How are path parameters used in a loader?
interview.answer: A route loader receives path parameters through its `params` object. The object keys are the parameter names, and its values come from the corresponding URL segments.
interview.followUp: What happens with `/posts/123/comments` for `/posts/$postId`? The parameter captures `123`; a child route can then express the remaining hierarchy.

interview.question: How can a component read a typed path parameter?
interview.answer: Use `Route.useParams()` in a route component to obtain the declared parameters without manually casting them. The route definition supplies the names and types to the generated hook.
interview.followUp: How can a parameter be made optional? Define it with the `{-$paramName}` form, which allows that URL segment to be omitted.

keyPoints: Declare a parameter by prefixing its name with `$`, such as `$postId`.
Loaders receive captured values in their `params` object.
Each parameter key matches the variable name used in the route path.
Parameter values come from the URL that matched the route.
The global `useParams` hook can read parsed parameters from components outside the declaring route.
Optional parameters use `{-$paramName}` so the segment can be omitted.
gotchas: A path parameter matches only one URL segment; it does not consume text across a slash.
When using the global hook outside a specific route, opt into the less-specific lookup with `strict: false`.
Use the optional-parameter syntax when the segment itself may be absent, rather than treating every parameter as required.

Routing fundamentals::Route trees.summary: Route trees map URLs to nested component trees, allowing layouts and child routes to mirror the UI hierarchy. TanStack Router supports file-based and code-based construction, with file-based routing recommended for less configuration.
Routing fundamentals::Route trees.explanation: A route tree is a nested structure that maps URL segments to a nested component tree. You can define it with file-based or code-based routing; code-based trees connect routes through parent relationships and are passed to the router.

parameters.name: routeTree
parameters.description: The route tree used by the router for route matching and component rendering.

example.title: Code-based route tree
example.explanation: A root route owns a child route, and the router receives the resulting tree for URL matching and rendering.

useCases.title: Compose nested layouts
useCases.scenario: An application has shared shells such as navigation, headers, or settings panels.

useCases.title: Use file-based routing
useCases.scenario: A team wants route structure to follow a routes directory and generate the tree.

useCases.title: Build routes in code
useCases.scenario: Routes must be declared explicitly in TypeScript or assembled dynamically.

interview.question: What is a route tree, and why is nesting useful?
interview.answer: A route tree is a nested route structure that TanStack Router uses to match a URL and render the corresponding nested component tree. The hierarchy lets parent layouts remain rendered while child routes render inside them.
interview.followUp: How can a code-based tree be assembled? Define routes with parent accessors such as getParentRoute, then attach them to a parent with addChildren before passing the result to createRouter.

interview.question: What are the two ways to build a route tree?
interview.answer: TanStack Router supports both file-based and code-based routing. They provide the same core routing capabilities, but file-based routing usually needs less code and is the recommended configuration style.
interview.followUp: When might code-based routing be useful? It can be appropriate when routes need to be declared programmatically rather than derived from a route-file convention.

interview.question: How does the router consume a route tree?
interview.answer: The router is created with a routeTree option. That option is the complete tree used to match routes and render components, whether the tree was generated from files or assembled in code.
interview.followUp: What should be checked if navigation cannot match a route? Verify that the intended route is included in the tree supplied to createRouter and that its parent relationship is correct.

keyPoints: The tree connects URL matching with the component hierarchy that gets rendered.
File-based and code-based route trees expose the same core routing capabilities.
File-based routing is the recommended default because it reduces configuration work.
Nested routes let a URL produce a nested UI structure rather than a single isolated component.
A route tree may combine flat route files and directory-based organization.
gotchas: For new applications, prefer file-based routing when it fits your project because it generally requires less configuration.

Search parameters::Links and active stat.summary: Build typed links from route definitions with to, params, and search. Control active matching with activeOptions and style matched links through activeProps.
Search parameters::Links and active stat.explanation: Define navigation with the Link component instead of constructing URLs manually: give it a route-relative or absolute to value and pass path parameters and search data through their dedicated options. Link determines activity from the destination pathname by default, can compare search parameters inclusively, and can apply activeProps when the current location matches.
Search parameters::Links and active stat.syntax: <Link to="/route" params={...} search={...} activeOptions={{ exact, includeSearch, includeHash }} activeProps={...} />

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Destination route path; do not place path, hash, or search parameters inside it.

parameters.name: params
parameters.description: Path-parameter object or updater function.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Search-parameter object or updater function.

parameters.name: activeOptions
parameters.type: { exact?: boolean; includeSearch?: boolean; includeHash?: boolean }
parameters.description: Controls exactness and whether search or hash values participate in active matching.

Search parameters::Links and active stat.returns: A rendered navigation link that updates the URL and exposes active or inactive styling props based on the current location.

example.title: Typed link with search-aware active styling
example.explanation: This typed link targets the products route, supplies a search value, and applies activeProps when the current URL inclusively matches that search.

useCases.title: Create route-safe links
useCases.scenario: Application navigation

useCases.title: Update query-string state
useCases.scenario: Filtered lists and pagination

useCases.title: Style the current route
useCases.scenario: Menus and breadcrumbs

useCases.title: Choose exact or inclusive activity
useCases.scenario: Parent and child routes

interview.question: How do you build a typed link with search parameters?
interview.answer: Use Link with a typed to destination and pass query data through search. Path parameters belong in params, while activeProps can add styling when the destination matches the current location.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve existing query values while changing one? Pass search a function that receives the previous search and returns a new object, typically by spreading the previous values before overriding one field.

interview.question: What determines whether a Link is active?
interview.answer: The link is active when its resulting pathname matches the current route; by default, a pathname prefix is sufficient. If search values are supplied, they are checked as an inclusive match unless activeOptions changes that behavior.
interview.followUp: How can a link ignore query-string differences? Omit search from the link or configure activeOptions so search matching is disabled.

interview.question: Which options control active-link behavior?
interview.answer: Use activeOptions to control matching details. The documented options include exact for child-route behavior, includeSearch for query matching, and includeHash for hash matching; activeProps and inactiveProps can style the result.
interview.followUp: When would exact be useful? It prevents a parent-route link from remaining active while a descendant route is displayed.

keyPoints: Use activeOptions to customize the conditions under which a link is considered active.
Set exact to true when the link should be active only at the destination route, excluding child routes.
includeSearch enables active matching against the search object using inclusive comparison.
Explicit undefined search properties can require that those keys be absent from the current URL.
Use the search prop to create or update query parameters through a link.
gotchas: Keep path parameters, search parameters, and hashes in params, search, and hash respectively; embedding them in to is unsupported.
Search matching is inclusive by default, so extra current search parameters do not make a link inactive. Configure activeOptions when exact search matching is required.
A differing hash does not affect active status unless includeHash is enabled.

Search parameters::Navigation blocking.summary: Navigation blocking prevents transitions away from a route, such as when an editor has unsaved work. Use a blocker predicate to decide when to pause navigation and custom resolver UI to let the user leave or stay.
Search parameters::Navigation blocking.explanation: TanStack Router can pause navigation through useBlocker when shouldBlockFn returns true. The predicate receives current and next locations, including route IDs, params, and search values; withResolver lets custom UI decide whether to proceed or reset. Browser unloads use the generic confirmation dialog, and confirmed unloads bypass blockers.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Required options object containing the blocking predicate and optional resolver and unload settings.

parameters.name: shouldBlockFn
parameters.description: Receives current and next locations and returns whether navigation should be blocked; may be asynchronous.

parameters.name: withResolver
parameters.description: Enables use of the resolver returned by the hook for custom confirmation UI.

Search parameters::Navigation blocking.returns: A blocker object exposing navigation state and, when resolver mode is enabled, controls such as proceed and reset.

example.title: Block leaving an editor
example.explanation: Blocks leaving the editor when its validated search state marks the work as dirty, then lets the user continue or cancel.

useCases.title: Protect unsaved work
useCases.scenario: A form or editor has changes that have not been saved.

useCases.title: Protect an in-progress workflow
useCases.scenario: A payment or other multi-step operation must finish before leaving.

useCases.title: Conditional destination blocking
useCases.scenario: A route should block only selected destinations or search states.

interview.question: How do you block navigation conditionally?
interview.answer: Use useBlocker with a shouldBlockFn predicate. Return true when the current and next locations match the condition that should pause navigation, such as leaving a dirty editor.
interview.followUp: How can the application present its own confirmation UI? Set withResolver so the hook exposes control for the UI to call proceed or reset.

interview.question: What information can the blocking predicate use?
interview.answer: The predicate can inspect current and next location data, including routeId, fullPath, params, and search. This lets blocking depend on both the destination and search state.
interview.followUp: How would you block only one destination? Compare next.fullPath or next.search values inside shouldBlockFn rather than blocking every navigation.

interview.question: How are multiple blockers and unloads handled?
interview.answer: Blockers are evaluated asynchronously and sequentially. A blocker that allows navigation lets later blockers run, while a blocker that cancels stops the remaining blocker functions.
interview.followUp: What happens during a browser refresh? The browser displays its generic leave dialog; confirming it bypasses all router blockers.

keyPoints: Navigation blocking pauses a route transition before it completes.
A dirty form or editor is a standard reason to protect the current route.
Multiple blockers run asynchronously in sequence rather than all deciding independently at once.
The router adds blockers around the underlying history API, so protected transitions are paused.
TanStack Router supports both hook-based logic and component-based blocking approaches.
gotchas: In-app blockers do not provide a custom dialog for browser unload actions; those actions use the browser's generic leave confirmation.
Returning false from a blocker cancels navigation, while a true result allows the remaining blockers to run.

Search parameters::Search middleware.summary: Search middleware transforms query parameters before links are generated and after navigation validation. TanStack Router provides retainSearchParams for preserving keys and stripSearchParams for removing keys or default-valued entries.
Search parameters::Search middleware.explanation: Search middleware transforms validated search parameters while generating links for a route or its descendants, and also runs during navigation. Use retainSearchParams to preserve selected or all keys, and stripSearchParams to remove selected keys or values matching defaults.

parameters.name: retainSearchParams input
parameters.description: Whether to retain every search parameter or an array of parameter names to retain.

parameters.name: stripSearchParams input
parameters.description: Whether to strip all parameters, an array of optional parameter names, or values matching a partial search object.

Search parameters::Search middleware.returns: A transformed search-parameter object used to generate links and process navigation.

example.title: Retain selected parameters and strip defaults
example.explanation: This route keeps rootValue in descendant links and removes page when it equals its default value.

useCases.title: Retain shared context
useCases.scenario: A root-level filter or tenant key must remain available when navigating to descendant routes.

useCases.title: Strip default values
useCases.scenario: Pagination or sorting values should disappear from URLs when they equal schema defaults.

useCases.title: Chain transformations
useCases.scenario: Several normalization rules must apply to every generated descendant link.

interview.question: When does search middleware run?
interview.answer: Search middleware transforms search parameters when generating links for a route or its descendants. It also runs after search validation during navigation, so the resulting query string is consistently normalized.
interview.followUp: How are multiple middleware functions applied? They are chained in order; each middleware receives the current search or the result passed through by the preceding middleware.

interview.question: How does retainSearchParams differ from stripSearchParams?
interview.answer: retainSearchParams accepts true or a list of keys. true keeps every search parameter, while a key list limits retention to the named parameters.
interview.followUp: How would you retain one parameter while removing a default page value? Chain retainSearchParams with stripSearchParams in the route's middleware array.

interview.question: What forms can stripSearchParams accept?
interview.answer: stripSearchParams can receive true, a list of keys, or an object matching part of the input search schema. An object removes values that deeply equal the configured defaults, which is useful for compact URLs.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to list-based stripping? Only optional search parameters may be named, because required parameters must remain valid.

keyPoints: Middleware changes the search object used to generate links belonging to a route and its descendants.
The same transformations are applied during navigation after validation, keeping generated URLs consistent.
Retention can be global with true or selective with an array of parameter names.
Stripping supports a boolean, a list of keys, or an object describing values to remove.
Use object-based stripping to omit default-valued parameters and make URLs less verbose.
Several middleware operations can be composed in one route configuration.
gotchas: A key-list passed to stripSearchParams can remove only optional search parameters; required keys cannot be listed.
retainSearchParams(true) preserves every search parameter, so use a key list when broad retention is undesirable.
Object-based stripping removes a parameter only when its value is deeply equal to the configured value.

Search parameters::Search validation.summary: Validate route search parameters with validateSearch to turn parsed URL values into a typed object. Schemas can enforce constraints and provide defaults or fallbacks for missing or invalid input.
Search parameters::Search validation.explanation: Attach a schema to a route through validateSearch. TanStack Router passes the parsed search object through that schema; the resulting values become typed route search state, while schema defaults or fallbacks handle absent or invalid values. Read the validated result with the route’s useSearch hook.

interview.question: What is validateSearch used for?
interview.answer: validateSearch receives the raw search parameters and returns the validated search object. Its return type is inferred through the router, so route consumers receive typed values.
interview.followUp: What happens when validation throws? The route enters an error state, and the error is thrown during rendering; recoverable URL input should use schema fallbacks where appropriate.

interview.question: How should defaults and optional values differ?
interview.answer: A schema can enforce constraints such as numeric bounds, allowed enum values, and required fields. Defaults provide values for missing input, while fallbacks can also protect against invalid input.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve a truly absent value? Use an optional schema field instead of assigning a default, then handle its possible undefined value in consumers.

interview.question: How do components consume validated search parameters?
interview.answer: Use the route’s useSearch hook to read the validated search state in its component. The values are typed according to the schema attached to that route.
interview.followUp: Can validated search values be used outside components? The documentation describes useSearch for route components and also for accessing validated search parameters elsewhere in the application.

Search parameters::Structural sharing of.explanation: Structural sharing reuses unchanged references in router state. With a fine-grained useSearch selector, changing one query parameter can replace only that parameter while preserving unrelated selected data, so components subscribed to the unchanged portion need not rerender. It is available globally through router configuration or locally on the hook.

interview.question: What does structural sharing do for search parameters?
interview.answer: Structural sharing preserves references for unchanged portions of router state between renders. For example, changing only `bar` can keep `search.foo` referentially stable while replacing `search.bar`.
interview.followUp: How would you limit rerenders to one search subset? Use `select` on `Route.useSearch` and enable structural sharing for the selected result.

interview.question: How can structural sharing be enabled?
interview.answer: Set `defaultStructuralSharing: true` in `createRouter` to enable it for fine-grained selectors throughout the router. Alternatively, pass `structuralSharing: true` to the relevant `useSearch` call.
interview.followUp: How can one route opt out when the global default is enabled? Pass `structuralSharing: false` for that hook usage.

interview.question: What restriction applies to selected values?
interview.answer: The selected value must be JSON-compatible because structural sharing compares and reuses JSON-like data. Returning class instances from a selector is not supported when the option is enabled.
interview.followUp: What should be done if a selector needs a non-JSON value under a global default? Disable structural sharing for that specific hook call.

keyPoints: The optimization reuses unchanged object or value references instead of recreating the whole search result on every navigation.

gotchas: Structural sharing is disabled by default, so explicitly enable it globally or on the individual hook when relying on this optimization.
A selector using structural sharing must return JSON-compatible data; class instances and other non-JSON values are unsuitable.

interview.question: How are search parameters supplied during typed navigation?
interview.answer: Use the navigation API's `search` option to pass query values. It accepts either a search object or a function that receives the previous search state and returns the next state.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve existing query values while changing one field? Use a functional `search` update and return the previous search object with the changed property overwritten.

interview.question: What makes search-parameter navigation type-safe?
interview.answer: The route's search configuration determines the expected query shape. TypeScript checks the values supplied to `search` and reports missing required parameters.
interview.followUp: What enables stronger checking for a route's search values? Define validation with the route's `validateSearch` option so the route exposes a typed search result.

interview.question: How do you preserve or modify search state during navigation?
interview.answer: Use `search={true}` on a Link when all current search parameters should be carried into the destination. For selective updates, use an object or updater function instead.
interview.followUp: How can a parameter be removed rather than retained? Set that parameter to `undefined` in the navigation update.
